title: Learning vs. Task-Completing
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart observes that many students can describe schoolish behaviors such as completing tasks and checking grades but cannot say what learning is or how to do it, and that teachers are often not much better because we plan lessons as sets of tasks. He points to the widespread, unsupported belief in learning styles as evidence of weak professional understanding of how learning works. His argument is that learning itself, which can open whole disciplines and shape identity, is a deep source of motivation that task-completion never taps. He urges teachers to teach this difference relentlessly, to direct their own professional development toward it, and to ask philosophical and pragmatic questions together, accepting that the change will be slow.
points: Students tend to equate school with task-completion and cannot explain what happens when they actually learn.
Teachers often plan in terms of tasks rather than in terms of how the brain learns, which is why myths like learning styles persist.
Learning, not compliance, is the real source of lasting motivation in a classroom.
Teaching the learning-versus-tasks distinction explicitly is a long-haul project for both teachers and students.
quotes: In other words, they are aware of schoolish behaviors. But they can’t tell you exactly what’s happening when they learn or how one goes about actually doing this learning thing.
I can hardly blame them. If we’re honest, most of us teachers aren’t much better at communicating the difference. We tend to think of lessons and units in terms of the tasks students will complete.

Heck, there’s not even agreement on what the learning style list should include! And yet we teach the theory to our students, to our parents, in our schools of education, in our professional development.
But learning is amazing. Learning can be emancipatory. Learning can open whole universes (for that’s what disciplines are). Learning can deepen and shape our very identity.

Ask hard, philosophical questions during the same hour that you ask hard, pragmatic ones. Think big and small at the same time, day by day, and the slow change will be that both you and your students will think more sharply about what school is for.
